statement: In adults entering one US residential research unit to come off opioids, 30 people whose urine showed fentanyl (enrolled 2021 to 2024) compared with 103 people who entered about a decade earlier with other opioids such as heroin (2010 to 2015), all given the same fixed morphine treatment (only the fentanyl cohort could also have other medicines for symptoms), were associated with more withdrawal while on that treatment: their self-rated withdrawal rose to a peak in the first days and then eased, while the earlier group's fell steadily from the first day; on four of the days severe self-rated withdrawal was 3 to 6 times as common (for example 47% against 8%); observers rated most of the fentanyl group as mildly withdrawn on most days against a small minority of the earlier group, though almost no one in either group was rated above moderate; and 43% against 19% had a fast heart rate at least once. Anxiety, aches, stomach symptoms, sweating and many other symptoms were all higher, with no single symptom explaining the difference. The comparison group came from another decade and another trial, the fentanyl group was older and could be given extra comfort medicines, ratings were not blind, and xylazine and other adulterants were not tested, so fentanyl cannot be shown to be the cause; the study also measured withdrawal during morphine treatment, not untreated withdrawal. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: People coming off illicit fentanyl in one research unit had worse withdrawal than people coming off heroin there ten years earlier, even though both got the same medicine. Their withdrawal got worse over the first days before easing, and fast heartbeats were more common. Because the two groups were from different times and the fentanyl group got extra medicines, we cannot be sure fentanyl itself caused the difference.
population: Adults with opioid use disorder entering a residential research unit in Baltimore for withdrawal management within two randomized trials; 133 people, 84% men, 56% Black
comparator: Urine positive for other opioids, no fentanyl, at entry about a decade earlier (2010 to 2015), with the same fixed morphine treatment on the same unit
outcome: Self-rated (SOWS) and observer-rated (COWS) withdrawal, its course over the stabilization days, heart rate, blood pressure and pupil size
magnitude: No effect sizes or confidence intervals reported. Severe self-rated withdrawal, fentanyl against earlier cohort: 48% against 16%, 47% against 8%, 37% against 6% and 27% against 6% on four consecutive days; observer-rated mild withdrawal 73% against 33% up to 73% against 18% on the following days; tachycardia at least once 43% against 19% (p < 0.05). statement: In emergency responders such as police officers and paramedics, evidence is insufficient to say whether, or how often, incidental contact with fentanyl or its analogues on the skin causes opioid toxicity (an overdose): no source on file measured responders' exposure or blood levels or counted poisonings among exposed responders, and none of the three, a position statement and two descriptive studies, documents a confirmed case. A 2017 position statement of two North American clinical-toxicology societies, the American College of Medical Toxicology (ACMT) and the American Academy of Clinical Toxicology (AACT) (Moss et al., 2017: eight authors from poison centres, universities, hospitals and a public health institute in the USA and Canada; the recommendations rest on the opinion and clinical experience of a task force of ACMT members and a literature search by the authors; reviewed by an ACMT committee, its board and its members and approved by both societies' boards; no funding and no conflicts of interest declared; filed here as a narrative review, so its figures are second-hand and no search method is given), measured no exposure, blood level or responder, and says that its recommendations mainly represent the consensus opinion of experts because data are limited. The two societies judged the risk of clinically significant exposure for responders to be extremely low, and incidental absorption through the skin unlikely (in the recommendations, very unlikely) to cause opioid toxicity. They wrote that they had not seen reports of responders developing signs or symptoms consistent with opioid toxicity from incidental contact, and that the reports they cite (a 2016 warning of the US Drug Enforcement Administration, with two 2017 news reports cited for responders' concern) described nonspecific symptoms, such as dizziness or a feeling that the body was shutting down, without objective signs such as slowed breathing; the incidents are not examined one by one and no count of exposures is given, so the statement could not have detected how often poisoning happens. Their reasoning is arithmetic for fentanyl, not measurement: with both palms covered by fentanyl skin patches, which are made to deliver the drug, about 14 minutes would be needed to absorb 100 micrograms, an amount the statement treats as a high dose without saying why it was chosen (editors' check: 425 micrograms an hour at the stated steady-state rate); they argue that powder or tablets on the skin are taken up more slowly than from a patch and can be brushed or washed off, so that toxicity, if it occurred, would not develop rapidly. At the highest airborne concentration met by industrial workers, an unprotected person would need nearly 200 minutes of exposure to reach a dose of 100 micrograms (inputs not stated, nor whether inhaled or absorbed), and the statement says that fentanyl's very low vapour pressure suggests evaporation from standing powder is not a practical concern. Splashes to the eyes or mouth are treated as a real route (absorption across mucous membranes more than 30 times that across skin, as stated; one case report of a veterinarian who became drowsy after a splash of carfentanil with xylazine, where the authors say the part played by carfentanil is unclear). No estimate is given for carfentanil, described as 10,000 times as potent as morphine in animals, or for any other analogue, although the conclusions cover them; the statement says that the analogues' physical properties suggest a potential for skin absorption and that pharmacological data on other analogues are limited. It concerns responders' incidental contact, not people who handle or use fentanyl regularly. It holds that toxicity cannot occur from simply being near the drug, and it still recommends nitrile gloves for routine handling, washing skin with water rather than with alcohol-based sanitizers, and, in the unusual case of significant airborne powder, a properly fitted N95 respirator or P100 mask, which it judges likely to give reasonable protection (its summary says an N95 gives sufficient protection in exceptional circumstances with drug particles or droplets in the air); it adds that individual practitioners may differ. The first data, both descriptive, also find no confirmed case, and neither could have found how often one occurs. A review of news reports (Herman et al., 2020: eight authors from an emergency medicine department at Johns Hopkins University, published as an editorial in the journal that carried the position statement, with the statement's last author as its senior author; no funding and no conflicts of interest declared) searched LexisNexis for English-language print and online news from North America published from January 2012 to March 2018: of 1,408 articles retrieved, 1,016 were on the topic and 214 described a specific responder's exposure to an opioid, and none of the 214 described a plausible route, symptoms consistent with opioid toxicity and confirmatory laboratory testing together. Only one incident, in 2016, mentioned any laboratory test of an exposed responder, a urine result reported as traces of opiates, which the authors explain probably came from an opiate screen, a test that does not detect fentanyl or its analogues and, in urine, reflects exposure over the previous several days rather than at the time. The unit is the article, not the incident (distinct incidents are not counted), each article was read by one of five reviewers against criteria the paper does not define, and only the three-part combination is reported, so the zero shows that the news did not report confirmation, mainly because testing was almost never mentioned, not what happened to the responders. A Health Hazard Evaluation by the US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH; Jackson et al., 2018) reconstructed one incident in early 2018 from records and from interviews four months later: during a vehicle search, white powder from a locked box blew into the faces of two officers, who within minutes reported difficulty breathing, dizziness and confusion, and a colleague gave one of them naloxone for what was described as shallow breathing and fading consciousness; emergency medical services then found both alert and oriented with normal oxygen saturation, and in the emergency department both had normal-sized pupils and normal heart and breathing rates, neither had any laboratory test, and both went home after more than an hour without symptoms. A field test of the seized substances was reported positive for fentanyl, but the state forensic laboratory identified cocaine, methamphetamine and THC and no fentanyl or other opioid. Nothing was measured on the officers or in the air, the powder reached their faces and one officer's nose, not only their skin, and their perceived risk was not assessed; the clinicians who examined them saw no objective signs of serious opioid toxicity, and NIOSH considers it possible that the non-specific symptoms reflected milder toxicity from some drug. In the same report NIOSH states, as its own position and citing the position statement among its sources, that a brief touch of fentanyl powder, or of an analogue, is not expected to be toxic when visible powder is quickly removed. Neither study can show that no responder has ever been poisoned: news reports are a selected record in which testing was almost never mentioned, and one incident gives no rate. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated (for the absence of a confirmed case only).
plain: In 2017, two North American societies of poison specialists said that an emergency responder, such as a police officer or paramedic, is very unlikely to be poisoned by brief, accidental contact with fentanyl on the skin. They had seen no reports of a responder with signs of an opioid overdose from such contact; the reports they cite described dizziness and similar feelings, without signs such as slowed breathing. Their view is expert opinion backed by arithmetic, not measurement: even with both palms covered in fentanyl skin patches, made to deliver the drug, it would take about 14 minutes to take in what they treat as a high dose. Powder splashed into the eyes or mouth is treated as a real risk, and no arithmetic was done for stronger analogues such as carfentanil. They still recommend gloves, washing skin with water, and a fitted mask when powder is in the air. The first real-world data point the same way but cannot settle it. In 214 news stories from 2012 to 2018 about police officers or paramedics exposed to opioids, none described a likely route, symptoms that fit an opioid overdose and a confirming lab test together; only one incident mentioned any test, a urine screen that probably cannot detect fentanyl. The stories were counted rather than the incidents, and one reviewer read each. In one incident looked into by a US federal workplace-safety agency, powder blew into two officers' faces in 2018 and they felt ill; their medical records showed no signs of a serious opioid overdose, neither was tested, and although a field test said fentanyl, the lab found cocaine and methamphetamine but no fentanyl or other opioid in the seized drugs. The agency says a brief touch of fentanyl powder is not expected to be toxic if visible powder is quickly removed. Neither study can show that no responder has ever been poisoned.
population: Emergency responders (law enforcement and emergency medical services) in North America who may meet fentanyl or fentanyl analogues as powder, tablets or liquid on calls, at crime scenes or in drug raids: as considered in a 2017 position statement, which studied no responders, exposures or cases; as reported in 214 English-language North American news articles (January 2012 to March 2018) that described a specific responder's exposure to an opioid; and two sheriff's department officers in one incident in early 2018, investigated afterwards by NIOSH
exposure: Incidental contact with fentanyl or its analogues: on the skin (the question here), and also airborne powder breathed in, splashes to the eyes or mouth, and being near the drug; reasoned from pharmacokinetic data in the position statement, as reported in news articles (routes recorded but not reported), and, in the NIOSH incident, white powder of unknown composition blown into two officers' faces; no source measured any exposure
comparator: None in any source: the position statement collected no data, and its worked arithmetic takes as its reference the time needed to absorb 100 micrograms of fentanyl through the skin, or the exposure needed to reach a dose of 100 micrograms from the air, an amount it does not justify; the news review and the incident investigation had no comparison group
outcome: Clinically significant opioid toxicity in the responder (objective signs such as slowed breathing or a lowered level of consciousness), as distinct from nonspecific symptoms such as dizziness or anxiety; in the news review, a confirmed exposure (an article describing a plausible route, symptoms consistent with opioid toxicity and confirmatory laboratory testing together); in the NIOSH incident, symptoms and clinical findings in emergency medical service and emergency department records, and forensic analysis of the seized substances
magnitude: No measured rate or count of poisonings. ACMT and AACT position (Moss et al., 2017): risk of clinically significant exposure extremely low; no reports seen of responders with signs or symptoms consistent with opioid toxicity from incidental contact; incidental skin absorption unlikely (summary) or very unlikely (recommendations) to cause toxicity. Worked arithmetic, fentanyl only: both palms covered by fentanyl patches (body surface 17,000 cm2, palm 0.5%, delivery 2.5 micrograms per cm2 per hour at steady state), about 14 minutes to absorb 100 micrograms (editors' check: 170 cm2 × 2.5 = 425 micrograms an hour, so 14.1 minutes); patches take 3–13 hours to give a therapeutic serum concentration and 35 hours to peak; at the highest airborne concentration met by industrial workers, nearly 200 minutes of exposure to reach a dose of 100 micrograms (inputs not stated, nor whether inhaled or absorbed); vapour pressure 4.6 × 10^-6 Pa. Mucous membranes: more than 30-fold the absorption of skin; one case report of drowsiness after a splash of carfentanil with xylazine, its cause unclear to the authors. No estimate for carfentanil (10,000 times as potent as morphine in animals) or any other analogue. Respiratory protection: an N95 respirator or P100 mask likely to give reasonable protection against significant airborne powder (recommendations); an N95 sufficient in exceptional circumstances with particles or droplets in the air (summary). Herman et al. (2020), English-language North American print and online news (LexisNexis), January 2012 to March 2018: 1,408 articles retrieved, 1,016 relevant (editors: 72%), 214 describing a specific responder exposure (editors: 21% of relevant); 0 of 214 with a plausible route, consistent symptoms and confirmatory laboratory testing together; any laboratory testing of an exposed person mentioned for 1 incident (2 articles; editors: 0.9% of 214), an opiate urine result; distinct incidents not counted, and no count reported for any single criterion. Jackson et al. (2018; NIOSH), 1 incident, 2 officers: no laboratory test of either officer; no objective signs of serious opioid toxicity in EMS or emergency department records (alert and oriented, normal oxygen saturation, normal-sized pupils, normal heart and respiratory rates in the emergency department, blood pressure raised); observed for more than an hour and discharged; naloxone given to one officer at the scene; seized items: cocaine, methamphetamine and THC identified, alprazolam and sodium bicarbonate only indicated, no fentanyl or other opioid, against a presumptive field result for fentanyl; no exposure measured.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_moss_2017 (editors' narrative-review checklist): overall high. The evidence was chosen by a task force after a literature search with no stated databases, dates, terms or criteria; the recommendations are, in the statement's own words, primarily consensus expert opinion; the absence of poisoned responders is the authors' observation, without a search record, a case series or a count of exposures; the incidents are represented by a DEA warning and news reports and are not examined one by one. Card sc_herman_2020 (JBI prevalence checklist, first pass): moderate for what the count describes, whether news articles reported a confirmed exposure: each article coded by one reviewer against undefined criteria, with no agreement statistic, distinct incidents not counted, and results given only for the three-part combination. Card sc_niosh_2018 (JBI checklist, first pass): high for any conclusion about cause: no biological, air or skin sample, a field test contradicted by the laboratory, no record of which item formed the cloud of powder, and an account reconstructed four months later. The three share one gap, the absence of any measurement of exposure, so one level, not two.

inconsistency.note: None: the position statement (from its authors' knowledge), the news review and the incident investigation all report no confirmed case; they differ in design and none estimates a rate.

indirectness.note: Second-hand and extrapolated in the position statement: the skin estimate uses fentanyl patch data, a steady-state rate through a matrix designed to deliver the drug, which the authors themselves say overstates uptake from powder or tablets; the air estimate uses industrial exposure data whose inputs are not given; both are for fentanyl only, with no figure for carfentanil or other analogues; the 100-microgram reference amount is not explained; and the statement concerns responders' incidental contact, not people who handle or use fentanyl regularly. The news review examined news text, not medical, police or laboratory records. In the NIOSH incident the powder reached the officers' faces and one officer's nose, not only their skin, and no opioid was identified in the seized items, so it bears on reported exposures in general, not on skin contact with fentanyl.

imprecision.note: Not rated separately: no source estimates a rate or count of poisonings among exposed responders (the news review counts articles, not exposures or incidents, and one incident has no denominator), a gap already counted under risk of bias; very low is the floor.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable. The news review describes the media's own selection (incidents that reached English-language news indexed by LexisNexis); that selection is counted under risk of bias and indirectness, not here.

grade.reasoning: Re-rated on 13 November with the first data on file, a review of news reports (Herman et al., 2020) and a NIOSH Health Hazard Evaluation (Jackson et al., 2018), both read from their PDFs. The claim no longer rests only on a narrative review, but its certainty stays very low and its relation insufficient evidence. All three sources are observational, so the start is low (METHODS §6.3): the news review is a case series of media-reported incidents, the evaluation a single case report, and the position statement, filed as a narrative review, starts from the design of what it describes (pharmacokinetic studies of fentanyl patches and of inhaled fentanyl, a patch product label, industrial exposure limits, one small volunteer study, one case report, one animal study and agency warnings, none randomized and none a study of exposed responders). Down one level for risk of bias: the statement's unsystematic selection and consensus opinion, the news review's undefined criteria applied by one reviewer per article with incidents not counted, and the evaluation's reconstruction from records and interviews four months later with nothing measured; all three share one gap, the absence of any measurement of exposure, so one level, not two. Down one for indirectness: patch and industrial data applied to powder on the skin (fentanyl only), news text instead of medical, police or laboratory records, and one incident in which the powder reached the officers' faces and no opioid was found in the seized items: very low, the floor, so imprecision (no source can give a rate) is not counted again. Inconsistency is now assessable and absent: none of the three reports a confirmed case. The new data do not raise the rating because both are descriptive records with no denominator of exposures: the news review's zero follows mainly from testing almost never being mentioned (one incident, two articles), so it shows that the news did not report confirmation, not that no responder was poisoned; and the evaluation tested neither officer, so it can neither confirm nor exclude poisoning in that incident, while its laboratory found no opioid in what was seized. The relation stays insufficient evidence: no source measured exposure, so neither poisoning from skin contact nor its absence can be shown with any precision, and none could have detected how often poisoning happens. The societies' judgment that the risk is extremely low and that skin absorption is unlikely, or very unlikely, to cause toxicity is reported as their judgment, with their own hedges (unlikely, very unlikely, likely to give reasonable protection), and NIOSH's statement on brief skin contact as NIOSH's own position, which cites the societies' statement among its sources; neither is adopted as the editors' finding. Where the statement's summary is firmer than the section it summarizes (an N95 gives sufficient protection, against an N95 or P100 likely to give reasonable protection), both are given. The single quotation records the statement's own description of its basis. Not used: the statement's naloxone section and NIOSH's recommendations (guidance, which this answer does not cover), the second-hand figures on deaths from synthetic opioids, and the news review's untested suggestions (a nocebo effect; protective equipment delaying care). Status replicated, for the absence of a confirmed case only (METHODS §6.4): two independent primary studies of different design, the news review (by a Johns Hopkins team whose senior author is the position statement's last author) and the NIOSH evaluation, agree that no confirmed opioid poisoning was documented, as the statement says from its authors' knowledge; none measured exposure, and none can show that no responder was ever poisoned. statement: In police officers and other emergency responders in the United States, surveyed at trainings in Missouri in 2019 (Winograd et al., 2020) and Indiana in 2020–2021 (del Pozo et al., 2021) and interviewed at five law enforcement agencies in 2020 (Attaway et al., 2021), the belief that touching fentanyl can cause an overdose was held by about 4 in 5 of those surveyed, and concern about it was voiced by nearly all of those interviewed who were asked; answers given just after a training that included a 10-minute module correcting it disagreed with it far more often, but these before-and-after comparisons, with no comparison group or later follow-up and many participants missing, cannot show that the training changed the belief, or for how long. The studies measured what responders believed and said, not what fentanyl does: whether touching fentanyl can cause an overdose is a separate question (see 'Can touching fentanyl make you overdose?': evidence insufficient, no confirmed case on file), and the papers call the belief false or misinformation on the strength of the 2017 position statement of two clinical-toxicology societies and similar sources, not their own data. Before a 2-hour overdose-response training in the Eastern Region of Missouri (11 sessions, January to August 2019, reaching 200 participants, of whom 140 were analysed: 113 law enforcement or security officers and 27 emergency medical or fire department workers), 20.9% answered False to the True/False item "I can overdose from touching fentanyl." (law enforcement 16.8%, 19 of 113; emergency medical 37.0%, 10 of 27; 29 of 140, 20.7%, by the editors' arithmetic), so about 4 in 5 did not. Before a 3-hour harm-reduction and occupational-safety training (SHIELD) held by Zoom for Indiana officers from December 2020 to June 2021 (204 attendees from 49 counties, of whom 129, 63.2%, answered the baseline survey), 103 of 129 (79.8%; Wilson 95% interval about 72% to 86%, editors' calculation) agreed, 52 of them strongly, with a 6-point item saying that first responders who encounter fentanyl are at great risk of overdose by touching or inhaling it; 79 of the 129 (61.2%) had earlier had fentanyl exposure precaution training. Neither sample was random: both were attendees of trainings in one Midwestern state each, answering a single unvalidated item. In interviews at five purposively chosen agencies (January to May 2020; 23 officers and leaders analysed, 20 of them asked open questions about fentanyl), nearly all of those asked said they were concerned that encountering fentanyl might put them at risk of an overdose and a few were not, with no counts given for any theme; they named other officers, law enforcement professional organizations, a 2016 Drug Enforcement Administration roll-call training video shown at in-service training, and regional intelligence bulletins as their sources; over one third of officers had heard of someone in their own agency overdosing, but none could say for certain that the substance was fentanyl or that the colleague had overdosed; two said they had been exposed themselves without symptoms; and a handful who were asked did not know the toxicology societies' statement. The interview study's abstract, saying that nearly all those interviewed wrongly believed skin contact was deadly, is sharper than its Results. In online US news found through Media Cloud for January 2015 to September 2019 (Beletsky et al., 2020), 506 of 551 relevant articles (92%) were coded as misinformation, a category that included any article giving an anecdotal account of an overdose blamed on casual contact, with its rumoured symptoms, so neutral incident reports counted, against 45 corrective or partially corrective articles, 18 of them unequivocally corrective; misinformation articles received 450,011 Facebook shares, against 48,235 for the corrective or partially corrective and 29,652 for the unequivocally corrective (about 15 to 1 against the last group, the abstract's figure, and about 9 to 1 against all 45, editors' calculation); the authors' potential reach of 69,751,705 is shares multiplied by an assumed 155 contacts, an upper bound on views, not a count of people, although the abstract presents it as people reached; and the two most-shared stories, as the authors summarize news reports, concerned two Ohio officers, one whose powder and overdose were never confirmed by laboratory testing and one whose substance was later confirmed as methamphetamine. Counting articles and shares cannot show that the coverage shaped officers' beliefs. Immediately after the Missouri training, which included about 10 minutes on contact with fentanyl, 83.6% answered False (law enforcement 81.4%, emergency medical 92.6%; 117 of 140 by the editors' arithmetic), so about 1 in 6 did not; of the 69 Indiana officers (53.5% of baseline respondents, 34% of attendees) who completed a follow-up linked to their baseline, 27 (39.1%; about 28% to 51%, editors' calculation) still agreed and 42 (60.9%) disagreed, 22 of them strongly, and their mean score moved from 2.2 to 4.0 on the scale from 1 (strongly agree) to 6 (strongly disagree) (paired t = 6.52, p < .001). Neither study had a comparison group or a later follow-up; the second answers came after the trainers had given the answer, from people who knew what was wanted; 43 of the 200 Missouri participants are unaccounted for and no paired counts are reported; two-thirds of the Indiana attendees are missing from its before-and-after comparison, whose abstract sets 79.8% of 129 against 39.1% of 69; and any change belongs to the whole training, not to the 10-minute module alone. The Indiana paper's printed effect sizes are wrong: its Cohen's d of 2.33 for the change is incompatible with its t and n, and by the editors' calculation the standardized change is about d_z = 0.78, the printed 2.33 matching the standard deviation of the paired differences and the printed interval [1.05, 0.51] matching that of d_z rather than that of the 1.8-point mean change (about 1.25 to 2.35). The two training studies share two authors (Goulka, Beletsky), and Beletsky is also first author of the media study; the trainings were developed or are delivered by the authors' teams, and both evaluations were publicly funded (in Missouri through the US Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, in Indiana through a CDC Overdose Data to Action grant). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: In two US surveys at trainings, about 4 in 5 police officers and other emergency workers thought touching fentanyl could make them overdose: before training, 103 of 129 Indiana officers agreed that responders are at great risk of overdose from touching or breathing it in (2020–2021), and only about 1 in 5 of 140 Missouri police and ambulance or fire workers said it was false that they could overdose from touching it (2019). In interviews at five US police forces in 2020, nearly all officers asked said they were worried; they named other officers, a 2016 training video from the US Drug Enforcement Administration and police bulletins as where they had heard it, and over a third had heard of a colleague overdosing, though none could say it was confirmed. Researchers counted 506 of 551 US news articles from 2015 to 2019 as misinformation, including plain reports of officers falling ill; these got about 450,000 Facebook shares, against under 30,000 for articles that clearly corrected it. Right after trainings that included a 10-minute lesson on fentanyl, far fewer still agreed: about 1 in 6 in Missouri, and 27 of the 69 Indiana officers who answered again. But nobody compared trained with untrained people or asked again later, many never answered a second time, and the Indiana paper printed its effect sizes wrongly. These studies show what people believed, not what touching fentanyl does.
population: Police officers and other emergency responders in the United States: 140 responders analysed (113 law enforcement or security officers and 27 emergency medical or fire department workers; mean age 40.96, 110 men) of 200 people reached by 11 overdose-response trainings in the Eastern Region of Missouri, January to August 2019; 129 of 204 Indiana officers from 49 counties who attended three SHIELD trainings held by Zoom between December 2020 and June 2021 and answered the baseline survey (mean age 45.1, 97 men), 69 of whom also answered the follow-up; 23 officers and agency leaders at five purposively chosen US law enforcement agencies, interviewed from January to May 2020, 20 of them asked about fentanyl; and, for news coverage, 551 online US news articles from January 2015 to September 2019
exposure: For the beliefs and their sources, none: what responders answered or said before any training, and online news articles coded for their message, with their Facebook shares; for the change, attending a training that included about 10 minutes of corrective information on contact with fentanyl (a 2-hour in-person overdose-response training in Missouri; a 3-hour SHIELD harm-reduction and occupational-safety training by Zoom in Indiana, led by a former police officer)
comparator: None outside the trainees: the same people's answers just before the training (in Missouri everyone analysed, with no paired counts reported; in Indiana the 69 linked completers); no untrained comparison group and no later follow-up; in the news study, corrective and partially corrective articles against misinformation articles
outcome: Answers to single belief items (True or False to a statement that they could overdose from touching fentanyl, in Missouri; agreement on a 6-point scale with an item that first responders who encounter fentanyl are at great risk of overdose by touching or inhaling it, in Indiana); concern about overdose from encountering fentanyl and the sources named, in interviews; for news articles, the authors' coding as misinformation, corrective or partially corrective, Facebook shares and modelled potential views

evidence.extracted: Between May and December 2019 the authors used Media Cloud, an open-source web-scraping media analysis tool, to identify mainstream online news published from January 2015 to September 2019, querying nine terms on casual fentanyl exposure (fentanyl AND glove*, mask*, touch*, contact*, absor*, inhal*, breath* or expos*); the results were reviewed for relevance and duplication, noting the state, the incidents covered and any reference to government guidance. Four trained reviewers (staff and student interns) coded redundantly, and a staff member resolved discordant codes. Potential reach was modelled from Facebook share counts (from Media Cloud via CrowdTangle) multiplied by an average person's number of contacts (155), which the authors call an upper bound on views, assuming that every sharer and contact saw the article and that no one saw more than one article on an incident. Editors' notes: there is no neutral category, so an article reporting an officer's account without endorsing it counts as misinformation; no agreement statistic between coders is reported.

Coverage and response: attendees of trainings, not samples drawn at random (Missouri: 140 of 200 analysed, 43 unexplained; Indiana: 129 of 204 at baseline and 69 at follow-up); interviewees picked by agency contacts at purposively chosen agencies, 3 of the 23 not asked. inconsistency.note: None: the two survey baselines agree (about 4 in 5) despite different items, states and years, the interviews agree without counts, and both before-and-after comparisons move the same way.

indirectness.note: Attendees of overdose-response and harm-reduction trainings in two Midwestern states in 2019 to 2021, and five agencies in 2020: how far they represent US police generally, or beliefs today, is unknown. The items ask about overdose, not death, and the Indiana item combines touching with inhaling. The second answers measure what people said right after a lesson, not lasting belief or behaviour at overdose scenes. The news study counts online articles and Facebook shares, not what officers saw or believed.

imprecision.note: Not rated down: the baseline intervals are moderately narrow (Indiana agreement about 72% to 86%; Missouri answering False about 15% to 28%, editors' calculation); the Indiana follow-up rests on 69 people (about 28% to 51%), an uncertainty smaller than that from the missing two-thirds, which is counted under risk of bias.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: two evaluations, each by a team that developed or delivers the training it evaluated, with no registration; an unpublished evaluation that found no change cannot be excluded, but none is known.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (METHODS §6.3): it reports how many responders said they held the belief, where they said it came from, how news coverage carried it, and how answers differed just after a training; it does not claim that training changed beliefs, which these designs cannot show. Descriptive, observational evidence starts low; down one level for risk of bias (training attendees rather than random samples, heavy missing data, single unvalidated items, second answers given straight after the corrective message, interviews without counts) and one for indirectness (two Midwestern states and five agencies in 2019 to 2021; items about overdose rather than death, one combining touching with inhaling; answers rather than behaviour): very low. Not upgraded: descriptive claims are never upgraded for a large effect, and the before-and-after shifts are not estimates of an effect. Rated as worded: as estimates of a training effect, both training studies are at critical risk of bias under ROBINS-I (no comparison group, an immediate post-test, attrition), so a claim that training changes the belief would also be very low, and the statement says that the designs cannot show it. The single quotation records the Missouri item itself, because its wording is the measure; the Indiana item, 17 words long, is paraphrased. Editors' calculations (Wilson intervals; counts from the printed group percentages; the recomputed standardized effects, d about 0.40 and 0.56 and d_z about 0.78; the interval for the paired change; the ratios of shares) are labelled for the second reader to recompute. Printed figures corrected or qualified: the Missouri overall 20.9% fits 29 of 139, not of 140 (20.7%), and its differences are percentage points; the Indiana Cohen's d values (2.33, 1.61, 2.33) are incompatible with the printed t and group sizes, its paired interval matches d_z rather than the mean change, and its printed patrol means contradict the stated direction; the Indiana abstract's 79.8% against 39.1% mixes denominators of 129 and 69 and calls a 3-hour training with a 10-minute module a 10-minute online training; the news study's 6.6% of total is 6.6% of misinformation shares (6.0% of all), and its 70 million people reached are an upper bound on views; and the interview study's abstract says more than its Results. Beliefs are reported as beliefs: the papers' description of the belief as false rests on the 2017 ACMT and AACT position statement and similar sources, and this project rates that question separately (very low certainty, insufficient evidence, no confirmed case on file), so the answer says what people believed, not whether they were right. Status replicated by the same team (METHODS §6.3, overlapping evidence): the two surveys that give numbers share two authors (Goulka, Beletsky), and Beletsky is also first author of the news study; the interview study shares no author with them (one of its authors and Beletsky list the same University of California, San Diego division) and agrees that concern was near universal among those asked, but without counts it cannot replicate the figures. Not used: the second-hand New York survey (nearly 80% believing that briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly), which is not on file, and the papers' views on stress, stigma, wasted resources and delayed overdose response, which they did not measure. Stays draft until a second reader has checked the anchors and the four first-pass cards are merged.
